post.title: LeScout: Feeding Coding Agents Less to Get More
post.description: How LeScout scouts foreign repos in a hardened Docker sandbox and compresses a project's whole context into one dense markdown file for agents.
post.excerpt: Coding agents waste context in two directions: unsafe, noisy repo ingestion and fresh sessions that re-derive everything. I built LeScout to sandbox the scouting and caveman-compress the context into one file an agent loads in a single read.
post.content:
I run coding agents all day, and I keep watching them waste context in two directions.

Inbound: when an agent needs to understand a foreign repo, the naive move is to git clone it onto your host. That is a security problem (postinstall hooks and setup scripts can execute untrusted code) and a context problem: the agent gets flooded with raw files.

Outbound: every fresh agent session spends dozens of turns re-deriving project context that a previous session already knew, and pre-loading all skill files burns thousands of tokens before work starts.

The trigger is written in the design doc (Plans/CONTEXT-DISCIPLINE.md), dated the day I built the tool: "It's often better to just open a new Claude Code chat and give the same task... [if the agent could] bring the high level parts, the agent can easily pick up where it left."

**LeScout** is the productization of that instinct. It is a local Bun/TypeScript CLI, part of the LeSearch AI family ("Less Search, More Agents"), MIT licensed. It scouts foreign repos inside a hardened Docker sandbox where only structured text ever crosses the boundary, and it "caveman-compresses" everything a knowledge brain knows about a project into one dense, token-budgeted markdown file that a fresh agent loads in a single read. Feeding agents less to get more.

## Install

There is no npm package and no build step. Install is clone plus symlink, and Bun runs the TypeScript directly:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/aryateja2106/lescout
cd lescout
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
ln -s "$PWD/bin/lescout" ~/.local/bin/lescout
docker build -t lescout/sandbox:latest docker/sandbox/
```

The bin/lescout wrapper resolves its own real path before exec, so the symlink can live in any directory on your PATH.

You need Bun 1.1 or newer, Docker (Colima works), and the GBrain CLI on your $PATH, or point GBRAIN_BIN at it. macOS or Linux. Sanity check:

```bash
lescout --version && lescout help
```

That prints 0.0.11 and a man page designed for agents to scan.

## It ate zod in 14.5 seconds

```bash
lescout repo https://github.com/colinhacks/zod --dry-run
```

On my machine this finished in 14.5 seconds: 608 files reduced to a depth-3 file tree, verbatim manifest copies, doc copies, and a TODO scan, with zero foreign code executed and a full audit envelope at ~/.lescout/runs/<run-id>/_run.json recording the exact docker invocation. Drop the --dry-run and the rendered markdown page lands in the brain via gbrain put.

## How it works

1. **Edge validation** (security.ts, a port of graphify's security.py philosophy). Before anything runs, the URL is checked against a host allowlist (github, gitlab, bitbucket, codeberg, sr.ht) and a protocol allowlist (http, https, git). Embedded credentials, control characters, and path traversal are rejected outright.

2. **Hardened sandbox** (sandbox.ts). The clone happens inside an Alpine 3.20 container run with --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, --no-new-privileges, --memory 1g with swap disabled, --cpus 1, --pids-limit 256, --ulimit nofile=1024, --user 1000:1000, a tmpfs scratch dir, --env-file /dev/null to hard-kill env inheritance, and a 120 second SIGKILL timeout.

3. **Defensive clone** (scout-repo.sh). Inside the container: a shallow clone with core.hooksPath=/dev/null and the credential helper cleared, so no foreign git hooks run and no host credentials leak. Then every file gets chmod -x, defense in depth even though nothing executes them anyway.

4. **Structured text out, nothing else**. Only four kinds of artifacts leave the container: tree.json, verbatim manifests (package.json, Cargo.toml, and friends), README/AGENTS/docs copies, and a ripgrep TODO/FIXME scan capped at 500 hits. The host parses those, renders a markdown page, and writes it to the brain.

5. **Audit everything**. Every run leaves _run.json with the exit code, timing, and the complete docker args list that was executed.

The hard rule: foreign code never executes on the host, and never executes in the sandbox either.

## Caveman-compress: the outbound half

```bash
lescout context lescout
```

Given a target name, context.ts runs a hybrid gbrain query plus slug-prefix sweeps over repos/, docs/, and sessions/, dedupes by slug, and enriches thin hits (under 500 chars) by fetching full pages: capped at 30 fetches, 5 KB per high-scoring hit, 2.5 KB for the rest. Hits are bucketed in a fixed priority order (docs > repos > sessions > notes > concepts > other) and rendered as one markdown file under a character budget: 30K tokens by default at a rough 4 chars per token, max 4,000 chars per item. The bundle lands at ~/.lescout/context/<target>-<date>.md, gets mirrored back into the brain, and is idempotent per day.

The name is honest engineering. There is no fancy summarization at read time, just ranked chunks brute-packed into one file under a hard budget. A fresh agent reads one file and picks up where the last one left off.

## The same discipline everywhere agents spend tokens

The pattern is always small index up front, full content on demand.

```bash
lescout session list --limit 3
```

session.ts knows the on-disk session layouts of six agent harnesses (Claude Code, pi, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, IBM Bob) and fully parses JSONL, including token usage and cost, for three of them. `lescout session resume <id>` writes a summary to the brain so any other agent can pick up the thread.

```bash
lescout skills list
```

The skill index reads only YAML front matter, a design target of roughly 100 tokens per skill, and loads a full body only on demand. The economics are visible in the output: on my machine one skill costs 4,875 tokens to load in full, another 190.

```bash
lescout store roots
```

store extends the idea into a read-only unified registry over all five artifact types (skills, MCPs, hooks, plugins, extensions) across every agent's scattered config locations. It ships a paranoid redaction layer: redact.ts matches provider key patterns for OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub, Google, Slack, and private keys, and beyond that treats ANY env value in an MCP config as a secret. False positives are cheap.

The whole tool is a deliberately thin composer: zero runtime npm dependencies, about 2,900 lines of TypeScript, and exactly three sanctioned shell-out targets, gbrain, docker, and git, a rule enforced in AGENTS.md. That file treats AI agents as first-class users and contributors. It tells agents not to git clone foreign repos themselves because that would put foreign code on the host, declares the sandbox flags sacred (--read-only, --cap-drop ALL, and --no-new-privileges may not be relaxed), and defines a Co-thought-with commit trailer for pair-worked commits. The README copies patterns, not codebases, from GBrain, Rowboat, Graphify, and AgentMemory.

Verify the suite yourself:

```bash
bun test
```

44 tests pass, 90 assertions, across redact, security, session, and skills.

## Honest limitations

Garbage in, garbage out. Bundle quality depends entirely on what is already in the brain. A live run today produced a 0-page bundle of roughly 162 tokens because the brain had no matching entries; the May bundles on this disk are 63 to 75 KB, so it works when fed. It fails loudly only when the gbrain binary is missing, not when results are empty.

It leans on a third-party brain. GBrain (Garry Tan, MIT) must be on $PATH. The native LeBrain on SQLite and FTS5 is a planned phase and does not exist yet.

The sandbox network is plain bridge. The container has ordinary internet egress, so isolation covers code execution and the filesystem, not exfiltration from inside the container. Per-host network allowlisting is deferred to Phase 2.

Smaller caveats: token budgeting is a crude 4 chars per token approximation, not a real tokenizer. Session parsing is full-fidelity only for Claude Code, pi, and Codex; Cursor, Gemini, and Bob are metadata-only. store is read-only, and `lescout docs` only handles GitHub repos. No npm publish, no releases: single-user and local-first by design. The docs have drifted from the code, too: the README understates the version, the test count, and the sandbox image size, so trust the CLI (0.0.11), bun test (44 passing), and the built image (51.5 MB).

And the big one: essentially all feature commits landed on a single day, 2026-05-15, with one backup snapshot since. This is a working v0, not a maintained product.

## What's next

Phase 2 is the honest gap list: per-host network allowlisting inside the sandbox, and install/remove/sync for the store. Phase 4 replaces GBrain with the native LeBrain on SQLite and FTS5, so the brain store stops being a third-party dependency.

One detail from the git log: the second-to-last commit reads "fix(phase-1.10+): apply 5 review findings (2 HIGH correctness, 1 HIGH security, 2 MED)". An agent review pass gated the GitHub push. The tool built to feed agents better context was itself shipped through one.

[Code is on GitHub](https://github.com/aryateja2106/lescout), MIT licensed.

I built LeScout, an open-source Bun/TypeScript CLI, to fix both directions.

Three takeaways:

1. Scouting runs in a hardened Docker sandbox: read-only, all capabilities dropped, env inheritance killed. Only structured text crosses the boundary. It processed zod's 608 files in 14.5 seconds with zero foreign code executed.

2. "Caveman-compress" packs everything the knowledge brain holds about a project into one token-budgeted markdown file. A fresh agent loads it in a single read and picks up where the last one left off.

3. The same discipline applies everywhere: skill indexes from YAML front matter instead of full bodies, session summaries any agent can resume, and a paranoid secret-redaction layer.

Zero runtime dependencies, about 2,900 lines of TypeScript, MIT.
